findings.title: Partial multi-seg packet corrupts TX ring state and mbuf ownership
findings.explanation: The jump to `end_of_tx` can happen partway through a multi-segment packet: the ring fills, a descriptor has len 0, or ioremap fails. By then earlier segments have advanced `txq->last_used`, been added to `tx_used`, and been stored in `sw_ring`, but `nb_tx` and `nb_tx_free` were not updated. If `nb_tx > 0`, `used_cnt` is published with trailing segments that have no EOP flag. The peer then joins them with the next packet. If `nb_tx == 0`, those slots are skipped without being published, so the next call writes used entries and `used_cnt` past descriptors the peer never sees filled. In both cases the caller still owns the unsent mbuf (it was not counted), while `sw_ring` points to it. `ntb_enqueue_cleanup` later frees it, which is a double free or use-after-free.
findings.suggestion: Check ring space for all `nb_segs` before touching any segment. On a mid-packet failure, roll back `txq->last_used` and `nb_mbufs` to where the packet started and clear the `sw_ring` entries written for it.

findings.title: RX loop reads past used_cnt on multi-segment packets
findings.explanation: `count` is capped by `used_nb`, which counts descriptors, not packets. The inner `while (true)` loop keeps consuming descriptors until it sees EOP, and never checks `rxq->last_used` against `used_cnt`. When multi-segment packets are pending (for example 4 descriptors holding 2 packets and count >= 4), the loop goes past the published entries. It reads stale used entries, hands back mbufs the peer has not filled, and takes descriptors the peer may be writing. If no EOP ever appears (a buggy peer, or stale entries), the loop wraps the ring and `rx_desc[nb_mbufs++]` overflows the stack array.
findings.suggestion: Track how many descriptors remain (`used_nb`). Stop or roll back when the inner loop would pass `used_cnt` without reaching EOP. Also bound `nb_mbufs` by the ring size.

findings.title: Allocation failure leaves the RX ring out of sync and leaks mbufs
findings.explanation: `rxq->last_used` is advanced before `rte_mbuf_raw_alloc`. If the allocation fails, the code jumps to `end_of_rx` without incrementing `nb_rx`. The received segment, and any earlier segments chained to `first`, are neither returned nor kept, so they leak and the packet is lost. If `nb_rx == 0` while some replacement mbufs were already allocated, `last_avail` has moved but `rx_desc` is never written to the ring. On the next call `avail_cnt` is published over those slots while the remote descriptors still point at old mbufs that were already handed to the application. The peer then writes into application-owned memory.
findings.suggestion: Allocate the replacement mbuf before consuming a used entry, or roll back `last_used` and `last_avail` on failure. Always publish the `rx_desc` entries that were filled, regardless of `nb_rx`.

findings.title: ioremap checks only the start address, so copies can run past the BAR
findings.explanation: `ntb_enqueue_bufs` writes up to `tx_item->len` bytes at the address this function returns. Both `addr` and `len` come from the descriptor ring, which the peer writes. The range check covers only `addr` and lets it equal `base + mw_size`, one byte past the window. A descriptor that sits near the end of the window, or has a large len, makes `rte_memcpy` write beyond the mapped BAR region. That corrupts other mappings or crashes the process.
findings.suggestion: Use `addr < peer_mw_base[i] + mw_size[i]`. Pass the length to ioremap (or check it in the caller) and reject any request where `addr + len` exceeds the window end.

findings.title: Write barrier is placed after the used_cnt publish, not before
findings.explanation: The packet data and used-ring entries are written into the peer's memory through the BAR, then `used_cnt` is updated, and only then does `rte_wmb()` run. BAR mappings are often write-combining, so the peer can see the new `used_cnt` before the data and used entries arrive and read stale lengths or flags. `ntb_queue_init` gets this right by issuing `rte_wmb()` before the count write.
findings.suggestion: Call `rte_wmb()` after the data and `tx_used_ring` copies and before `*txq->used_cnt = txq->last_used;`.

findings.title: avail_cnt is published before the write barrier
findings.explanation: The new descriptors are written to the remote `rx_desc_ring` through the BAR, then `avail_cnt` is updated, and only then does `rte_wmb()` run. The peer can see the new `avail_cnt` before the descriptor addresses and lengths arrive. It may then transmit to stale addresses or treat len 0 as an error.
